title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Substantive extension-selection prompt
The following customized prompt defines the extension-selection task used in preparing this plan:

I am creating a regression case study in R and Quarto. My question is: To what extent do incident type, institution size, and event year help predict reported economic losses from cyber incidents at financial institutions? The response is natural log of positive reported monetary loss in nominal USD. Predictors are incident type (physical or error, misuse or social, hacking or malware), institution size (up to 1,000 or over 1,000 employees), and incident year centered at 2013. The course-based core model is lm(log_loss ~ type + size + year_c). We have 26 incidents from 2002 to 2016. The baseline R-squared is 0.260. The estimated geometric mean loss ratio for larger versus smaller institutions is 12.0, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.28 to 521.5. Only five records involve smaller institutions, and none of those have misuse or social incidents. Suggest three feasible beyond-course extensions that strengthen this same regression question. For each, explain how it helps, how its result would enter the case study, the implementation steps, and two independent checks. Keep repeated cross-validation and influence sensitivity as the two separate course-method elements. Do not choose for me.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Options and our decision

Interactive regression display: Let readers choose predictors and see the predicted log loss and its uncertainty. Fit the model in R, make a small prediction grid, and add controls to the case-study page. Check the displayed values against R output and a manual calculation. This directly addresses our communication need.
Tree-based comparator: Fit a small random forest and compare log-loss RMSE with the regression using the same grouped folds. Check fold membership and compare its predictions with a simple reference model. With only 26 records, this may be unstable.
Model explanation display: Show how each regression term changes a selected prediction. Build it from the coefficient values. Check that the contributions sum to the prediction and compare factor coding with R’s model matrix. This may be less useful than directly showing uncertainty.

Selected extension: An interactive display of the baseline regression predictions and uncertainty. This adds a communication feature beyond the static regression output. It will support the course model, not replace either required course-method element.
Accepted: Use the interactive display to show how predictions and uncertainty change across observed predictor values.
Changed: Use predicted natural log loss as the main scale. If we also exponentiate it, label that value as the predicted geometric mean loss, not the arithmetic mean dollar loss. A confidence interval for the mean log response is not a prediction interval for an individual incident.
Not selected: The random forest comparator, because the sample is small. We also did not select the term-contribution display because the prediction display better addresses our main communication need.

title: AI Use and Verification
section: Implementation and connection to the case study
text:
Implementation and connection to the case study

Keep the same cleaned data, factor levels, and regression formula.
Create a prediction grid in R for the three incident types, two size groups, and years from 2002 to 2016. Use predict(baseline, newdata, interval = "confidence", level = 0.95).
Add a small interactive HTML/JavaScript display to the case-study page. Show the fitted log loss, its 95% confidence interval, and the number of records in the selected type-size group. Clearly flag groups with no observations and avoid predictions beyond the observed year range.
Put the display and a short interpretation in the case study’s “AI-supported extension” section. Explain which comparisons have wide intervals and little data. The feature will help readers judge how much the model can tell us about the same research question.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Two planned independent verification checks

Compare the display with R: Save predictions from predict.lm for a fixed set of combinations, including both size groups and every incident type. Compare the displayed fit and both interval endpoints with those saved values to numerical tolerance before rounding. Also test the controls, the year limits, and the warning for a group with no observations. Use the official R predict.lm documentation to confirm what the confidence interval represents. Result: pending.
Manual calculation: For a supported example, construct the model row x and calculate the fit as x times the coefficient vector. Calculate its standard error as sqrt(x V x’), using V = vcov(baseline), and the 95% interval with the t critical value and 21 residual degrees of freedom. Compare these results with R and the display. If we show dollar values, check the exponentiation separately. This uses a separate calculation rather than another AI answer. Result: pending.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Remaining limitation
The display cannot fix the small, selected sample or missing loss data. Some institutions appear more than once. The confidence intervals depend on the regression assumptions, and predictions for groups with little data may be unreliable. We will not make causal claims or use this model to recommend a security budget.

title: AI Use and Verification
text:
Other AI use
We used ChatGPT/Codex earlier to help find public data and check data availability. For this checkpoint, Codex also helped transfer the proposal into the website, prepare the preliminary AI plan, render the Quarto files, and publish and test the site. The planned extension and its independent verification are still pending.

Group members: Fernanda Lopez, Emiliano Santacruz, and Aidee Mendez.
AI-use plan and verification

title: Predicting Reported Cyber Incident Losses in Financial Institutions
text:
Question and audience
To what extent do incident type, institution size, and event year help predict reported economic losses from cyber incidents at financial institutions?
Our audience is risk management and cybersecurity teams at financial institutions. We want to understand which incident characteristics help explain differences in reported losses. This is a first step toward our longer-term interest in how banks divide resources between technology protection and financial protection. This project will not estimate an optimal security budget or the effect of buying insurance.
The response is reported monetary loss per incident. The candidate predictors are incident type, institution size measured by employee-count category, and incident year. We use the database’s broad information-security scope, including hacking, malware, information misuse, social engineering, and incidents involving lost devices or disclosure errors. Financial institutions include banks, payment firms, brokers, and insurers.

title: Predicting Reported Cyber Incident Losses in Financial Institutions
text:
Data
We use the VERIS Community Database (VCDB), which contains publicly disclosed security incidents coded by community contributors using the VERIS framework. Our source is a fixed repository version, accessed October 23, 2026. The observational unit is one incident record. The validated-data folder contains 10,047 records, including 893 with finance-and-insurance industry codes beginning with NAICS 52. Of those, 61 have a positive overall loss recorded. We embed those 61 records and 11 relevant source fields below so the QMD can run without a separate data file or an internet connection.
Keeping only losses explicitly coded as USD gives 35 records. Requiring a known employee-count category and incident year leaves 28. We exclude two records after reviewing their meaning. The JPMorgan record uses a $250 million annual cybersecurity budget as its loss amount. The Cignet record uses a fine for denying access to medical records and failing to cooperate with an investigation. Neither measures a loss from the incident described in that record. The reasons are supported by JPMorgan’s 2014 annual report and the HHS Cignet case description. Our final sample has 26 incidents from 2002 to 2016.
The response comes from impact.overall_amount, with currency checked using impact.iso_currency_code. It includes recorded financial consequences such as theft, settlements, and fines. These amounts do not necessarily measure the full loss or the amount ultimately paid by the institution. We keep nominal USD as coded in VCDB without adjusting for inflation. Size comes from victim.employee_count: up to 1,000 employees versus over 1,000, following the VERIS size definitions. Year comes from timeline.incident.year and may be the start of an event that lasted several years.
We group incident types before fitting the model. Records with hacking or malware go into “Hacking or malware.” Among the remaining records, those with misuse or social engineering go into “Misuse or social.” The rest go into “Physical or error.” This priority rule puts each record in one group when several actions appear together.
VCDB uses a CC BY-SA 4.0 license, which allows sharing with attribution and the same license for adapted data. The embedded data are shared under that license. We include incident IDs but no customer or employee identifiers. Public reports are not a random sample, and most financial-sector records have no usable loss amount. Some institutions appear repeatedly. Missing data, possible coding errors, different loss definitions, and the small sample limit generalization. We do not treat a missing loss as zero.

Figure 1: Reported losses for the 26 retained incidents. Each point is one record. The vertical axis uses a logarithmic scale. Boxes show the middle half of each group and lines mark medians.





The sample median loss is $10,500,000 for hacking or malware, compared with $465,000 for physical incidents or errors. Losses vary widely within each group, and only six records are in the hacking-or-malware group. These are differences in reported records, so the figure does not show that incident type causes a particular loss.

title: Predicting Reported Cyber Incident Losses in Financial Institutions
text:
Baseline model
We start with an additive linear regression of the natural log of reported loss on incident type, size category, and incident year. The log scale is useful because the retained losses range from $300 to $185 million. We center year at 2013 to make the intercept easier to understand. This model gives a simple starting comparison for all three predictors without adding interactions.


Show code
baseline <- lm(log_loss ~ type + size + year_c, data = analysis)
ci <- confint(baseline, level = 0.95)
terms <- c("typeMisuse or social", "typeHacking or malware",
           "sizeOver 1,000", "year_c")
results <- data.frame(
  Comparison = c("Misuse/social vs. physical/error",
                 "Hacking/malware vs. physical/error",
                 "Over 1,000 vs. up to 1,000 employees",
                 "One year later"),
  `Loss ratio` = exp(coef(baseline)[terms]),
  `95% CI lower` = exp(ci[terms, 1]),
  `95% CI upper` = exp(ci[terms, 2]),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL
)
knitr::kable(results, digits = 2, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))

Holding recorded incident type and year constant, the model estimates a geometric mean reported loss about 12.0 times as large for institutions with over 1,000 employees as for smaller institutions. The model-based 95% confidence interval for this ratio is 0.28 to 521.5. The point estimate is positive, but the interval includes 1 and is very wide, so this sample does not give a clear estimate of the size difference. This is a ratio of geometric means, not a dollar difference or a ratio of arithmetic mean losses.
A specific limitation is that only five incidents involve smaller institutions, and none of those five are in the misuse-or-social group. The adjusted comparisons therefore have limited overlap. The model explains about 26% of variation in log loss within this sample, but that does not measure performance on new incidents. The confidence intervals also assume independent errors, which may be questionable when institutions appear repeatedly.

title: Predicting Reported Cyber Incident Losses in Financial Institutions
text:
Where the analysis could go

Validation and comparison: We plan to compare the additive model with an intercept-only model using repeated five-fold cross-validation. Both models will use the same folds, and we will compare root mean squared prediction error on the log-loss scale. Records from the same institution should stay in the same fold after we check and standardize organization names from the source. This will help us assess whether the predictors improve prediction beyond a constant log-loss estimate.
Diagnostics and robustness: We plan an influence sensitivity analysis. We will use Cook’s distance to identify influential records, check their source descriptions, and refit the model with and without those records. We will compare the size and incident-type ratios and their intervals. Valid large losses will remain in the main analysis; the alternative fits will show how much the conclusions depend on individual records. This goes beyond showing routine diagnostic plots.

For the later AI-supported extension, one possible direction is an interactive display of model predictions and uncertainty. We would choose the extension after the course-based analysis and avoid predictions for combinations with little data. The extension would support the regression results and would need two independent verification checks.

title: Predicting Reported Cyber Incident Losses in Financial Institutions
text:
AI-supported extension plan
We plan an interactive display of the baseline model’s predicted log loss and 95% confidence interval. Readers will choose incident type, size, and a year within the observed range. Unsupported combinations will be flagged. We will show its main result on this page and check it against R predictions and a manual calculation. See the AI-use record.
